orientation.summary: Ohio's 2015 State Wildlife Action Plan (SWAP) is a statewide biodiversity conservation strategy produced by the Ohio Department of Natural Resources Division of Wildlife, covering Species of Greatest Conservation Need (SGCN) across 15 habitat categories. The document acknowledges climate change as a threat throughout, and includes a dedicated Chapter 5 on climate change that summarizes regional climate projections, vulnerability concepts (exposure, sensitivity, adaptive capacity), and a table of broad adaptation strategies. Engagement with range shift science is moderate but largely derivative — the document references external vulnerability assessments and literature (notably Staudinger et al., in review) rather than performing its own modeling, and explicitly states that climate change work during the plan period will focus on 'data collection and planning.' Conservation actions related to connectivity, habitat protection, and invasive species control are framed as indirectly helping mitigate climate change impacts, but targeted range-shift facilitation actions are largely absent.

evidence_index.text: Climate change vulnerability is comprised of three separate but related components -exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity. Exposure is a reflection of the type, degree, and duration of climate induced change. The degree to which the effects of that change are felt is related to the sensitivity of the object being acted upon. Adaptive capacity is a measure of object's ability to persist in the face of the change.
evidence_index.location: Chapter 5, Regional Species and Habitats at Greatest Risk

evidence_index.text: Climate change vulnerability studies for the Northeast and Midwest regions scored freshwater mussels, amphibians, and fish as either extremely or highly vulnerable, while the majority of birds and mammals received low vulnerability rankings. Similar studies focused on habitat vulnerability classified spruce-fir, lowland conifer, Appalachian northern hardwood forests, bogs, fens, and freshwater aquatic habitats as highly vulnerable to climate change.

evidence_index.text: Climate Change Vulnerability Assessments (CCVAs) have already been conducted for a number of species and habitats across the Northeast and Midwestern region. evidence_index.text: Predictions are that species' distributions will shift northward, upslope, and upstream, and the species that rely on them will either shift in response or adapt in place. These shifts will not happen at the same time, as species respond to different cues and at different paces. Shifts will be influenced by degree of habitat connectivity, as well as life history traits or genetic diversity that influence movement or adaptation.

projects: Snowshoe hare reintroduction (2000-2013, northeastern Ohio): 740+ hares translocated from Michigan and Maine; annual track-count monitoring found repatriation was unsuccessful, providing negative evidence for this approach under current habitat conditions in Ohio.
